Description: explicit — client-side hypsometric tint (color-relief layer, GL JS 5.6+)
prompt: I have terrain tiles as a raster-dem source in MapLibre GL JS and I want to color the map by elevation ranges (a hypsometric tint) directly client-side — blues at sea level through greens and browns to white peaks — without pre-rendering colored raster tiles. What layer type do I use and how do I configure the color ramp?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** *Use a **`color-relief`** layer.* It reads the same `raster-dem` source you already have and lets you tint the terrain client-side with an `interpolate` expression that works on the special `["elevation"]` value. Below is a complete, ready-to-copy example that shows: 1. Adding the DEM source (if you haven’t already). 2. Adding a `color-relief` layer that maps elevation → colour (sea-level blues → low-land greens → mid-mountain browns → snow-white peaks). 3. Optional tweaks (opacity, exaggeration, etc.). --- ## 1. DEM source (raster-dem) ```js // Add the DEM source – this is the same source you use for hillshade or terrain map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://tiles.example.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.webp', // or a TileJSON URL tileSize: 256, // default, keep it if you’re not sure encoding: 'terrarium', // or 'mapbox' – must match the tiles you serve maxzoom: 12 // whatever your DEM tiles support }); ``` > **Note** – The source can be reused by any elevation-based layer (`hillshade`, `color-relief`, `setTerrain()`). You only need one `raster-dem` source. --- ## 2. Hypsometric (elevation-tint) layer – `color-relief` ```js map.addLayer({ id: 'hypsometric-tint', type: 'color-relief', // <-- THIS IS THE KEY source: 'terrain-dem', // the raster-dem source defined above paint: { // The colour ramp – an interpolate expression over the special ["elevation"] value 'color-relief-color': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], // linear interpolation between stops ['elevation'], // <-- only works inside color-relief-color // ── elevation (meters) ── ── colour ─────────────────────── 0, '#2c7bb6', // deep ocean – dark blue 50, '#3b8cc4', // shallow water – lighter blue 200, '#5fa5d0', // near-shore – cyan-ish 500, '#a1d99b', // low land – light green 1000, '#74c476', // foothills – medium green 1500, '#31a354', // mid-elevation – darker green 2000, '#addd8e', // sub-alpine – yellow-green 2500, '#fdae61', // alpine – orange-brown 3000, '#d95f0e', // high alpine – reddish-brown 3500, '#a63603', // near-summit – dark brown 4000, '#ffffff' // snow-cap – white ], // Optional: make the tint semi-transparent so underlying imagery can still be seen 'color-relief-opacity': 0.85 } }); ``` ### How the ramp works | Elevation (m) | Colour (hex) | Visual meaning | |---------------|--------------|----------------| | **0** | `#2c7bb6` | Deep ocean (dark blue) | | **50-200** | `#3b8cc4` → `#5fa5d0` | Shallow water / coast | | **200-500** | `#a1d99b` | Low-lying land (light green) | | **500-1500** | `#74c476` → `#31a354` | Forested hills (greens) | | **1500-2500** | `#fdae61` → `#d95f0e` | Alpine rock (orange-brown) | | **2500-3500** | `#a63603` | Bare rock / dark soil | | **≥ 4000** | `#ffffff` | Snow / ice caps | *Feel free to adjust the stops, colours, or interpolation mode (`linear`, `exponential`, `cubic-bezier`) to match the palette you want.* --- ## 3. Full minimal example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre – Hypsometric Tint
``` *Run the page, tilt the map (mouse-drag while holding **Shift** or use the UI controls), and you’ll see the terrain coloured by the ramp you defined.* --- ## 4. Quick checklist – “Did I miss anything?” | ✅ | Item | |---|------| | **Layer type** | `type: "color-relief"` (only this layer type can colour a `raster-dem`). | | **Source** | Must be a `raster-dem` source (the same one you use for hillshade/terrain). | | **Expression** | Use `["elevation"]` **inside** the `color-relief-color` paint property; it is *not* valid elsewhere. | | **Ramp** | Build an `interpolate` (or `step`) expression with elevation stops → hex/rgba colours. | | **Opacity** | `color-relief-opacity` (default 1). Set < 1 if you want underlying imagery to show through. | | **Version** | `color-relief` was introduced in **MapLibre GL JS 5.6** – make sure you’re on that version or newer. | | **No pre-rendered tiles** | Because the colourisation happens on the client, you don’t need any “colored raster” tiles. | --- ### TL;DR ```json { "id": "hypsometric-tint", "type": "color-relief", "source": "terrain-dem", "paint": { "color-relief-color": [ "interpolate", ["linear"], ["elevation"], 0, "#2c7bb6", 200, "#a1d99b", 1000, "#74c476", 1500, "#31a354", 2500, "#fdae61", 3500, "#a63603", 4000, "#ffffff" ], "color-relief-opacity": 0.9 } } ``` Add that layer after your DEM source, tilt the map (or enable 3-D terrain) and you’ll have a smooth hypsometric tint rendered entirely on the client. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh” A **single** `hillshade` layer is already enough to give you a shaded-relief background. Harshness usually comes from one (or more) of these paint settings: | Property | What it does | Typical harsh-looking value | Softer alternative | |----------|--------------|----------------------------|--------------------| | `hillshade-method` | How the light is computed | `standard` (default) – a single light source that creates very dark shadows and very bright highlights | `multidirectional` (one pass, several light directions) **or** `igor` (minimises contrast) | | `hillshade-exaggeration` | Scales the slope-derived shading | `0.5` (default) – can be too strong on steep terrain | `0.3 – 0.4` | | `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Azimuth of the light (degrees clockwise from north) | `335` (default) – can put the light in a “top-left” spot that makes shadows look black | Any value you like, but you usually don’t need to change it when you switch to `multidirectional` | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Whether the light follows the viewport or the map | `viewport` (default) – the light stays fixed to the screen, which can feel unnatural when you rotate the map | `map` – makes the light rotate with the map (optional) | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Base colors for shadows / highlights | `#000000` / `#FFFFFF` (opaque) – pure black / white give the “chalky” look | Add an alpha channel and use warmer / cooler tones (e.g. `rgba(30,40,80,0.45)` for shadows, `rgba(255,240,200,0.4)` for highlights) | > **Do not stack multiple hillshade layers** to fake a multi-directional light. Since MapLibre GL JS 5.5 you can get the same effect with a single layer and the `hillshade-method` property, which is far cheaper performance-wise. --- ## Step-by-Step Fix 1. **Make sure you are on a recent MapLibre version** (≥ 5.5). The `hillshade-method` property was added in 5.5 and the `multidirectional` option in 5.5-5.6. 2. **Replace (or edit) your hillshade layer** with the following style. Adjust the colors/alpha to match your map’s visual language. ```json { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", "source": "terrain-dem", // <-- your raster-dem source "paint": { // 1️⃣ Use a multi-directional light to soften contrast "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", // 2️⃣ Reduce overall contrast a bit "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35, // 3️⃣ (Optional) Make the light rotate with the map instead of the viewport "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // 4️⃣ Warm, semi-transparent shadows "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)", // 5️⃣ Soft, warm highlights "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)" } } ``` ### What each line does | Line | Effect | |------|--------| | `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` | Lights the terrain from several directions in **one draw pass**, eliminating the stark black-white contrast of the default single-light method. | | `"hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35` | Lowers the intensity of the shading. Feel free to tweak between `0.25` and `0.45` until the relief looks natural. | | `"hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"` | (Optional) Ties the light direction to the map’s bearing, so the shading rotates as you rotate the map – often feels more “real”. | | `"hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)"` | Dark shadows with a bluish tint and 45 % opacity, which blends into the underlying imagery instead of turning pure black. | | `"hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)"` | Light highlights with a warm, slightly transparent hue, preventing the white-out effect. | 3. **Reload the style** (or call `map.setStyle()` again) and watch the hillshade soften instantly. 4. **Fine-tune** if needed: - **More contrast?** Raise `hillshade-exaggeration` a little (e.g. `0.4`). - **Even softer?** Lower it further or increase the alpha on the shadow/highlight colors. - **Different mood?** Swap the shadow/highlight colors for cooler or warmer palettes (e.g. `rgba(20,30,70,0.5)` for shadows, `rgba(255,250,220,0.3)` for highlights). --- ## Quick Checklist – “Did I miss anything?” - [ ] **Only one hillshade layer** for the DEM source. - [ ] `hillshade-method` set to `multidirectional` **or** `igor`. - [ ] `hillshade-exaggeration` ≤ 0.5 (lower if still harsh). - [ ] Shadow & highlight colors include an **alpha** value (≤ 0.5 works well). - [ ] No stray `raster` layer pointing at the DEM (that would just show the raw RGB tiles). - [ ] Using MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.5 (otherwise `hillshade-method` is ignored). If after these changes the hillshade still feels too strong, double-check that you haven’t accidentally added a second hillshade layer elsewhere in the style (e.g., in a different style file or via `addLayer` later in your code). Remove or merge it. --- ### Example: Full Minimal Map Setup ```html Soft Hillshade Demo
``` Open the page, pan/rotate, and you should see a **soft, natural-looking hillshade** under the satellite imagery. --- ## TL;DR 1. **Use one hillshade layer.** 2. Set `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` (or `"igor"`). 3. Lower `"hillshade-exaggeration"` to ~`0.3-0.4`. 4. Give shadow/highlight colors an alpha and a warm/cool tint. 5. (Optional) `"hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"` for rotating light. That’s all you need to turn a harsh, black-and-white hillshade into a smooth, terrain-aware backdrop. Happy mapping!
